channel.description: Recent content in Identity and Security on Layer5 Documentation

item.title: Keychains
item.description:
In Layer5 Cloud, a collection of permissions is represented as a keychain. One or more keychains are grouped together and assigned to a role. Later, a role can be assigned to a user. This is the general flow of how keychains reach a user.

  • A key allows one action, such as Create Token.
  • A keychain groups related keys, such as everything needed to manage teams.
  • A role groups keychains, and users hold roles in an organization or team.

A user’s effective keys in an organization are the union of the keys in every keychain of every role the user holds there. A keychain grants nothing by itself. It takes effect only through a role that includes it.

item.title: Keys
item.description:
In Layer5 Cloud, permissions are represented as keys, each serving as a unique identifier for a specific permission. One or more keys can be grouped together and assigned to a keychain. Then this keychain can be assigned to a role and that role can be assigned to a user. A user never receives a key directly. This is the general flow of how keys reach a user.

Keys, keychains, and roles are defined once for the whole Layer5 Cloud deployment. They are not copied or customized per organization. What varies per organization is which roles a user holds there. A user’s effective keys in an organization are the union of the keys from every role they hold in that organization, so the same person can hold a key in one organization and lack it in another. Holding an additional role only adds keys. It never removes any. Provider Admin holds every key and passes every check in every organization. For how this fits with authentication and cross-organization resource sharing, see Security Boundaries.

item.title: Sessions
item.description:
What sessions are 🔗

A session is the credential Layer5 Cloud issues each time someone signs in. It is what keeps a browser tab, a second device, or a connected Meshery Server signed in, and it is what you end when you want one of those sign-ins to stop working. Sessions expire on their own. API tokens do not.

Layer5 Cloud sessions use OAuth 2.0 for authentication. OAuth 2.0 is a standard protocol for authorization and focuses on client developer simplicity while providing specific authorization flows for web applications, desktop applications, mobile phones, and so on.

item.title: Tokens
item.description:
What tokens are 🔗

An API token lets software act as you. Scripts, CI/CD pipelines, mesheryctl, and other Meshery clients present it to Layer5 Cloud instead of signing in through a browser. Because a token carries your full authority and never expires, deciding how many tokens to create, who holds them, and when to delete them is a security decision.

A token is a credential bound to your user account. A client sends it as a bearer token in the Authorization header of each request. The Cloud API reference shows the exact form.
